strengths: Clear motivation with concrete demonstration of LLM-as-judge failures (overthinking, loops, invalid outputs) in Section 3.1 and Figures 4-6
Strong empirical data efficiency results: achieves comparable or better performance than discriminative PRMs trained on ~100x more data (8K vs 712K labels)
Computationally efficient training: only 4.5 hours on single A100 GPU with LoRA finetuning
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple dimensions: 6 benchmarks, multiple model sizes (1.5B-32B), multiple scaling scenarios (best-of-N, beam search, parallel/sequential)
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging overconfidence, step label interference, and computational overhead
Well-organized presentation with clear research questions (RQ1-RQ3) and effective visualizations
Ablation studies validating design choices (process vs. outcome-based filtering in Section 5.2, performance with more training data)
Out-of-domain generalization tested on physics and code despite training only on math
weaknesses: Experiment scale limitations: only 100/500 problems from MATH-500 (acknowledged in E.5), ~20 AIME problems, 86 GPQA problems; this undermines generalization claims

Unfair baseline comparisons: off-the-shelf PRMs (MathShepherd, RLHFFlow) use different base models; different generators used across experiments (Llama-3.2-3B vs Qwen-2.5-14B), confounding factors with approach contribution

Insufficient investigation of synthetic data quality: authors note 'spurious chains may still exist' but don't analyze what makes chains good beyond format+label matching; no deeper investigation of failure modes
No prompt sensitivity analysis: Table 3 shows LLM-as-judge varies 3-4 points by prompt, but THINKPRM's prompt sensitivity not systematically investigated despite emphasis on this as advantage

Overstated scaling benefits: Figure 20 shows parallel scaling plateaus quickly (K=8 similar to K=4); Figure 21 shows minimal sequential scaling gains; practical utility of scaling verification compute is limited
QwQ training issues unresolved: Section C.1 notes QwQ is 'hard to train with LoRA and still generates relatively high percentage of invalid judgments after training' but doesn't address this
Step-label interference (Section 5.4) identified but not analyzed: unclear whether this affects certain step positions more, or how prevalent it is
Limited true out-of-domain evaluation: trained only on math, tested on physics/code; real OOD would test on fundamentally different domains; modest OOD improvements (4.5-8%)
Framing concerns: '1% of process labels' is somewhat misleading about the actual data efficiency; strong label imbalance in Table 1 (92.3% correct) not discussed
Missing ablations: no intermediate data scaling studies (only 1K vs 65K), no investigation of whether reasoning model capability affects PRM quality

strengths: Clear identification and systematic documentation of LLM-as-judge limitations (overthinking, looping, invalid outputs) with concrete evidence
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME '24, GPQA, LiveCodeBench) with multiple test-time scaling scenarios
Well-motivated problem of data efficiency in PRM training; reducing label requirements by ~100x addresses practical deployment concerns
Principled synthetic data filtering using process labels rather than outcome labels, validated through ablation studies
Honest and detailed discussion of limitations (overconfidence, step label interference, computational overhead) in Section 5.4
Practical efficiency: training requires only 4.5 hours on single A100 GPU
Sound evaluation methodology with appropriate baselines (DiscPRM, LLM-as-Judge, majority voting) and multiple model sizes
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is straightforward fine-tuning of reasoning models on synthetic data, primarily applying existing techniques to a new model class rather than developing new methods
Evaluation uses reduced benchmarks undermining generalization claims: only 100/500 MATH problems, subset of GPQA-Diamond (86 questions), 200/thousands LiveCodeBench; no significance testing provided

Unfair comparison framing: emphasizes 100x label reduction vs DiscPRM while using different training objectives (LM loss vs BCE), multiple epochs, and model sizes; DiscPRM not designed for low-data regimes
Modest out-of-domain performance (8% GPQA-physics, 4.5% LiveCodeBench) raises generalization concerns despite training exclusively on math data; distribution shift not deeply analyzed

Critical score calibration issues unaddressed: P(token)-based scoring causes overconfidence with scores clustering near extremes, known to be problematic for reward models but dismissed as future work

Synthetic data quality concerns inadequately addressed: reliance on QwQ-32B (which exhibits its own issues), exact-match filtering may miss valid reasoning, acknowledged spurious chains not investigated

Step label interference failure mode (Section 5.4) only briefly mentioned but not investigated: if step i is marked incorrect, subsequent steps more likely marked incorrect; frequency and severity unknown
Arbitrary design choices lack justification: why 1K training examples? why 4096 token cutoff? why these trigger phrases? appears to be engineering choices without principled optimization

Evaluation methodology limitations: prompt sensitivity shown to vary wildly (50.6%→77.7% Table 3) but THINKPRM sensitivity not explored; generator model dependency explored minimally; no human evaluation of verification quality
Unfair comparison on data efficiency: synthetic chain filtering uses PRM800K process labels, so approach leverages existing supervision rather than being truly label-efficient
Sequential scaling evaluation extremely limited: only 200 OmniMath problems tested for sequential mode despite claiming this is an advantage
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars on any reported results

Incomplete experimental analysis: no error analysis of where THINKPRM fails vs DiscPRM, limited ablation on verification chain length importance, no analysis of computational cost trade-offs despite acknowledged overhead

strengths: Significant practical contribution: 100x reduction in required process labels (from ~700K to 8K) while improving performance across multiple benchmarks

Comprehensive evaluation with both in-domain (ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME'24) and out-of-domain tasks (GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench), including multiple test-time scaling scenarios (best-of-N, beam search, parallel/sequential verification)
Thorough empirical work with proper ablations: process vs outcome filtering validation (Section 5.2), training data scaling analysis (Figs 22-23), and difficulty-based performance analysis (Fig 12)
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear motivation, informative figures, example outputs, promised code/data release, and detailed hyperparameters in appendix
Identifies and documents real failure modes of LLM-as-a-Judge (overthinking, infinite looping, invalid outputs) with histogram evidence (Fig 4), providing valuable empirical insights
Very efficient training: 4.5 hours for 32B model on single A100, making approach practically accessible
Honest treatment of limitations: clearly discusses overconfidence, step label interference, and computational overhead in Section 5.4
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core contribution (fine-tuning reasoning models on synthetic data) is relatively straightforward; while well-executed, the insight that reasoning models can verify reasoning is intuitive

Filtering dependency: method critically relies on having gold step-level labels for filtering synthetic data; acknowledged workaround via Monte Carlo rollouts mentioned but not demonstrated, limiting claimed generality of 'minimal supervision'
Out-of-domain evaluation on small subsets weakens generalization claims: GPQA-Diamond uses only 86 physics problems and LiveCodeBench only 200 problems; larger OOD benchmarks would be more convincing
Incomplete evaluation scale: MATH-500 results use 100-problem subset (not full 500) due to compute constraints; ProcessBench thoroughly evaluated on only 2K problems from 2 subsets

Possible baseline issues: DiscPRM performance appears lower than some prior work; unclear if gaps stem from generative vs discriminative approaches or training setup differences; would benefit from showing generative-trained discriminative models

Calibration and interference issues noted but not deeply investigated: Section 5.4 acknowledges 'overconfidence' (extreme score clustering) and 'step label interference' (error propagation), but these receive limited analysis despite being important for deployment
Sequential vs parallel scaling comparison underdeveloped: Figure 21 shows no clear winner but only tests K=2,4; limited investigation into when practitioners should use which approach

True cost of synthetic data collection underexplored: Figure 22-23 show improvements with 65K examples but require many more samples; detailed cost analysis of data generation (running QwQ-32B inference) missing

strengths: Dramatic improvement in data efficiency: achieves competitive performance with only 8K step labels compared to discriminative PRMs trained on 712K labels (100x reduction), validated through comprehensive scaling curves

Thorough empirical evaluation spanning multiple benchmarks (ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME '24, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench), model sizes (1.5B-32B), and test-time scaling scenarios (best-of-N, beam search, parallel/sequential scaling)

Strong out-of-domain generalization: generative PRMs consistently outperform discriminative baselines under domain shift (8% gain on GPQA-Physics, 4.5% on LiveCodeBench), revealing robustness limitations of discriminative approaches

Well-motivated problem analysis: §3.1 provides concrete empirical evidence of LLM-as-judge failures (overthinking, invalid outputs, infinite looping) with supporting visualizations (Figs. 4-5) that clearly motivate the proposed solution

Principled methodology with solid ablations: process-based filtering (matching step judgments to gold labels) convincingly shown superior to outcome-based filtering (Fig. 9); data collection pipeline well-designed and clearly documented
Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges overconfidence clustering, step label interference, and computational overhead without dismissing them; demonstrates awareness of method's constraints
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (finetuning on synthetic data, process supervision, reasoning models) without substantial methodological innovation; inspiration explicitly from prior work (Yu et al., Kang et al.) on reducing overthinking
Modest performance gains on main benchmarks: MATH-500 best-of-N improvements ~2-3% over DiscPRM (Fig. 7); AIME '24 ~5% gain; suggests method is practical but not transformative in performance terms

Experimental scope constraints significantly limit generalizability claims: MATH-500 evaluation uses only 100/500 problems due to compute budget; AIME '24, GPQA-Physics, LiveCodeBench are small datasets; no reported confidence intervals or error bars

Training data characterization misleading: requires ~5K QwQ-32B samples (20% yield) and still depends on gold step labels from PRM800K for filtering; 'minimal supervision' framing is relative to discriminative PRMs but not truly label-efficient

Incomplete analysis of key phenomena: step label interference (§5.7) identified but not thoroughly investigated—occurrence frequency, impact magnitude unexplored; overconfidence clustering acknowledged but not addressed; score calibration issues (E.1) not analyzed

QwQ-32B training challenges inadequately addressed: LoRA fine-tuning still produces 15.1% invalid judgments (Table 2); authors acknowledge difficulty but don't explore full fine-tuning or alternative approaches
Test-time computational cost not analyzed: generating 1K-5K token verification CoTs is expensive compared to discriminative scoring; no latency comparisons or throughput analysis provided

Missing mechanistic understanding: limited intuition for why generative verification helps on hard problems (§5.5 analysis superficial); parallel vs. sequential scaling comparison (Fig. 20) yields no clear winner, leaving open questions about deployment strategy

strengths: Addresses practically important problem of data-efficient PRM training with clear 100x reduction in required supervision
Well-motivated analysis of LLM-as-judge limitations with concrete examples of failure modes (overthinking, infinite loops, invalid outputs)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME), model sizes (1.5B-32B), and evaluation scenarios (best-of-N, beam search)
Demonstrates respectable out-of-domain generalization (8% improvement on GPQA-physics, 4.5% on LiveCodeBench despite training only on math)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations (overconfidence, step label interference, inference overhead)
Thoughtful process-based filtering strategy shown empirically important via ablation
weaknesses: Limited core novelty—primarily applies established techniques (rejection sampling + finetuning) to new domain; lacks fundamental methodological innovation

Problematic baseline comparisons: (1) DiscPRM baselines trained by authors show suspiciously weak results (5.0 F1 on Table 2); unclear if this matches published PRM training procedures; (2) Comparisons with published PRMs confound data efficiency with architectural/training differences
Overstated generalization claims: 8% and 4.5% improvements only on small OOD subsets (86 and 200 examples) without error bars; long-form verification tested on single generator

Insufficient analysis of why approach works: no explanation for why longer CoT verification is fundamentally better beyond 'more compute'; mechanism of process-based filtering not analyzed; step label interference acknowledged but not explained
Incomplete computational cost accounting: inference overhead 'mentioned but not quantified'; token budget comparisons may not reflect real deployment constraints or fair comparison of wall-clock time
Small-scale experiments: MATH-500 uses only 100 problems (not full 500); GPQA 86 problems; no error bars or significance tests; percentage-point differences lack statistical rigor

Missing critical ablations: no analysis of 4K token constraint for synthetic data; QwQ with LoRA still produces 16% invalid judgments but full finetuning not attempted; limited exploration of prompt sensitivity
Reproducibility concerns: depends on preview models (QwQ-32B-Preview); no code release; unclear if approach generalizes to non-Qwen models

strengths: Substantial practical contribution: Achieves superior performance with 100x fewer process labels (8K vs 712K), directly addressing a major bottleneck in PRM training
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (ProcessBench, MATH-500, AIME '24, GPQA, LiveCodeBench) and test scenarios (best-of-N, beam search, parallel/sequential scaling)
Clear problem motivation: §3.1 provides compelling quantitative evidence for LLM-as-a-Judge limitations through overthinking analysis, invalid output measurement, and prompt sensitivity

Strong and consistent results: Outperforms both discriminative PRMs and LLM-as-a-Judge across all configurations; demonstrates OOD generalization (8% improvement on GPQA despite math-only training) and generalization to long-form reasoning
Practical training pipeline: Lightweight (4.5 hours on single A100), sensible process-based filtering, works with automatic labels, detailed reproducibility information
Honest limitations discussion: Transparently addresses overconfidence, step label interference, and inference overhead without dismissing contributions
Thoughtful ablations and analyses: Process vs outcome filtering (§5.6), automatic labels validation (§5.4), difficulty-based performance analysis (§5.5), compute-matched comparisons (§5.3)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core technique is rejection sampling finetuning (existing method); main contribution is empirical validation in new context rather than methodological innovation; missing algorithmic insights

Overstated supervision claims: Claims of 'minimal supervision' misleading—process-level labels still required for strict filtering criterion; filtering is domain-specific and doesn't scale naturally to new domains without validation data

Evaluation scope limitations: Uses only 100/500 MATH-500 problems (20%), 86 GPQA examples, 200 LiveCodeBench examples due to computational constraints; no confidence intervals or significance testing reported; limits confidence in generalization claims

Incomplete comparisons: GenRM mentioned but not directly compared; DiscPRM trained only 1 epoch (optimal tuning unclear); QwQ substantial underperformance (73.2% vs 86.5%) unexplained; missing comparisons to other recent generative verifiers

Score extraction method is ad-hoc: Using P('yes')/P('yes')+P('no') lacks justification; forced decoding of 'Is the solution correct?' appears unprincipled; no ablation on alternative scoring methods; authors acknowledge overconfidence but don't explore solutions

Unclear scaling strategy guidance: Figure 20 shows parallel vs sequential scaling has 'no clear winner'; limits claimed flexibility; no principled guidance for practitioners on when to use each strategy

Missing critical analyses: No investigation of what behavioral changes occur during finetuning; unclear why 8K labels outperform 712K (architectural vs training dynamics); no false negative analysis of filtering; limited error analysis

Inference cost not quantified: No wall-clock time or FLOPs comparisons between THINKPRM and DiscPRM despite generative verification being substantially more expensive; practical deployment trade-offs unclear
Training robustness concerns: QwQ noted as 'hard to train with LoRA' and still produces 15.1% invalid judgments; suggests potential stability issues not fully explored

Generalization questions remain: All synthetic data from QwQ-32B-Preview (cross-model robustness unclear); strong math results but weaker code improvements (4.5%); scalability to domains without step-level labels not demonstrated
